# Personal Statement — Makena Community Fund

My goal is an associate degree in electrical engineering technology from Kiptown Technical
College, followed by the utility lineworker certification program that the college runs with
Verandale Municipal Power. I settled on this path in a specific place: the storm season two
years ago, when my neighborhood in East Verandale lost power for nine days and the crews who
restored it were all contracted from out of the region. I spent that week helping my uncle
run extension cords from the one generator on our block, and I decided I wanted to be one of
the people a town does not have to import.

My financial circumstances are these. My mother works as a home health aide at twenty-two
hours a week, which is the maximum her own health allows, and her income covers rent and
part of our food. I work twenty-five hours a week at the Harwick Avenue grocery, and my
paycheck covers the remainder of the household costs plus my transit pass. After those
obligations I can save about forty dollars a month. Tuition for the program is $3,850 a
semester. At my current saving rate, the first semester alone would take eight years to
save for. I am not describing hardship for sympathy; I am showing the arithmetic that makes
this award the difference between enrolling next fall and not enrolling.

For the last three years I have volunteered with the East Verandale Tool Library, a lending
program run out of the community center on Prosper Street. I started as a Saturday desk
volunteer and now maintain the inventory system and train new volunteers — we lend roughly
sixty tools a week to about two hundred registered households. Last spring I organized the
library's first repair clinic, where volunteers fixed forty-one household items in one
afternoon, and we have run it monthly since. The center's coordinator, Ms. Adisa, can
confirm the dates and numbers.

What this award changes is simple and mechanical. It covers first-year tuition, which means
I can cut my grocery hours to fifteen a week, which is what makes attending daytime labs
possible at all — the program does not offer an evening section. Without the award I would
not attend more slowly; I would not attend, because the labs and my current work schedule
cannot coexist. With it, I enroll in the fall, keep my transit pass, and keep my Saturday
shift at the tool library, which I have no intention of giving up.

payload.text:
# Personal Statement — Makena Community Fund

Ever since I was young I have been passionate about science and helping people. I believe
that education is the key to unlocking a brighter future, and I am determined to pursue my
dreams no matter what obstacles stand in my way. Receiving this scholarship would mean the
world to me and would bring me one step closer to achieving my goals.

My family has faced financial challenges, as many families have. Money has always been
tight, and paying for college will be difficult. I know that with hard work and dedication,
anything is possible, but financial support would ease the burden on my family and allow me
to focus on my studies.

I have always been involved in my community and enjoy giving back. Helping others is
something I find very rewarding, and I have participated in various volunteer activities
throughout high school. These experiences have taught me the value of service and shaped me
into the person I am today.

This scholarship would allow me to attend college and pursue a degree in a STEM field. I am
excited about the future and confident that I will make the most of every opportunity. I am
committed to working hard, giving back to my community, and making a difference in the
world. Thank you for considering my application.

payload.text:
# Personal Statement — Makena Community Fund

I intend to complete a bachelor's degree in civil engineering at Northbay State, with a
focus on water infrastructure, and to return to work for the Tarrenton County water
district, where I have interned for two summers. The goal is specific because the problem
is: Tarrenton's distribution system loses an estimated thirty percent of treated water to
leaks, and the district's own engineering staff is three people, two of whom retire within
five years. My internship supervisor has told me plainly that the district hires from
Northbay's program when it can, and rarely can.

On community involvement: through my school's chapter of the Streamkeepers program I have
done quarterly water quality sampling on Miller Creek since tenth grade — that is eleven
sampling rounds, each logged with the county extension office, and our chapter's data was
cited in the district's culvert replacement application last year. I also taught the
sampling protocol to the incoming cohort this fall, six students.

I will be direct about what I am not including. My family's financial situation is not
something I am willing to lay out in a document that many people will read, beyond saying
that I qualify for the federal Pell Grant, which the committee can verify from my FAFSA, and
that the gap between total aid and Northbay's in-state cost of attendance is $4,100 a year.
I understand this application asks me to articulate need, and I understand a reviewer may
count this section against me. I would rather be counted down for reticence than perform
hardship.

The award covers most of that gap for one year. What it changes is not whether I attend
Northbay — I will attend regardless, on loans if necessary — but whether I graduate with
debt small enough to make a county water district salary a viable choice over the private
consulting offers that pull every Northbay graduate away from exactly the places that need
them. The award does not buy my attendance. It buys where I can afford to work afterward.
